message.content:
### The “core” of pop‑song harmony In most contemporary pop songs the harmonic palette is **very small** – usually just a handful of diatonic triads (and sometimes a few borrowed or secondary‑dominant chords). Because of this, a handful of chord progressions have become almost universal. Below is a quick‑look at the most common chords and the progressions that use them. | Key | Common diatonic triads (Roman numerals) | Typical pop progressions | |-----|----------------------------------------|--------------------------| | Major | I – ii – iii – IV – V – vi – vii° | I–V–vi–IV (Axis of Awesome)
I–vi–IV–V
ii–V–I
I–IV–V | | Minor | i – ii° – III – iv – v – VI – VII | i–iv–v
i–VI–III–VII (the “minor 4‑chord” progression)
i–VII–VI–VII | > **Why these chords?** > • They are all diatonic to the key, so they sound “natural” and easy to resolve. > • They cover the full range of emotional colors (major vs. minor, tonic vs. dominant). > • They are simple enough that listeners can pick up the pattern quickly, which is a hallmark of pop music. --- ## 1. The “Axis of Awesome” 4‑chord progression **I – V – vi – IV** - **Example songs:** - *Let It Be* (C – G – Am – F) - *Someone Like You* (A – E – F#m – D) - *Poker Face* (C – G – Am – F) This progression is the most ubiquitous in pop because it balances tension (V) and resolution (I) while giving a nice emotional lift with the vi chord. --- ## 2. The “I–vi–IV–V” progression - **Example songs:** - *Stand By Me* (C – Am – F – G) - *All of Me* (C – Am – F – G) It’s essentially the same four chords as the Axis progression but in a different order, giving a slightly more “classic” feel. --- ## 3. The “ii–V–I” progression - **Example songs:** - *Just the Way You Are* (F – G – C) - *I Want to Hold Your Hand* (Dm – G – C) This is a jazz‑influenced progression that adds a little more harmonic interest while still staying within the pop framework. --- ## 4. The “I–IV–V” progression - **Example songs:** - *Twist and Shout* (C – F – G) - *La Bamba* (C – F – G) The classic “three‑chord” progression that dates back to early rock & roll and still works in modern pop. --- ## 5. Minor‑key equivalents - **i–iv–v** (e.g., *Zombie* – Em – C – G) - **i–VI–III–VII** (e.g., *Apologize* – Am – F – C – G) These give a darker, more introspective mood while still using only diatonic chords. --- ## Quick cheat‑sheet for songwriting | Function | Major key | Minor key | |----------|-----------|-----------| | Tonic | I (C) | i (Am) | | Subdominant | IV (F) | iv (Dm) | | Dominant | V (G) | v (Em) | | Relative minor | vi (Am) | VI (F) | | Submediant | ii (Dm) | ii° (B°) | | Mediant | iii (Em) | III (C) | | Leading tone | vii° (B°) | VII (G) | **Tip:** Start with one of the four‑chord progressions above, then add a single “color” chord (e.g., a secondary dominant like V/V or a borrowed chord like ii°) to spice things up. --- ### Bottom line - **Most common chords:** I, V, vi, IV (major); i, iv, v, VI (minor). - **Most common progressions:** I–V–vi–IV, I–vi–IV–V, ii–V–I, I–IV–V. - **Why they work:** They’re diatonic, emotionally resonant, and instantly recognizable to listeners. Happy writing!
